shortDescription: India’s clean-mobility debate is usually staged as a contest between machines: batteries against cylinders, electric against CNG. It is the wrong contest. children: India’s clean-mobility debate is usually staged as a contest between machines: batteries against cylinders, electric against CNG. It is the wrong contest. The better question is what vehicle runs on, and where that energy comes from and the answer could lead to the paddy fields of Punjab and Haryana.

Numbers are encouraging but incomplete. Electric vehicles make up about 11 per cent of all vehicle sales in 2026, and nearly 43 per cent of passenger three-wheelers sold in the first seven months of this year were electric. For short, stop-start city trips, the battery is winning. But electric buses were under 5 per cent of sales and heavy trucks just 0.4 per cent.

An electric vehicle is also only as clean as the power that charges it. Coal and lignite supplied about two-thirds of India’s electricity in the July to September quarter of FY 2026, and officials expect coal to provide about half of generation as late as 2035-36.

This is why a recent TERI study on vehicular emission becomes important. It compared petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity and LNG across six vehicle categories over their full life cycles. Electric mobility offered favourable economics for two- and three-wheelers and certain urban uses, while CNG gave a competitive mix of affordability, life-cycle performance and practicality for cars, taxis, buses and several light commercial applications. The life-cycle record of EVs remains sensitive to electricity generation and battery manufacturing. The lesson is not one fuel, but the right fuel for each vehicle.

That is where compressed biogas (CBG) fits in. It is produced by digesting crop residue, dung and organic waste in sealed tanks, making CBG interchangeable with CNG, which can run through the same pipelines and engines. TERI’s earlier assessment found it can be carbon-negative: up to 1.141 kg of CO₂ equivalent avoided per kilometre for a four-wheeler, the result of avoided methane leakage from unmanaged dung and of digestate replacing synthetic fertiliser. The study estimates that blending 20 % CBG into CNG could make the fuel carbon-neutral over its life cycle. Same fact was also highlighted by Niti Aayog in its Net Zero Report for the Transport Sector released in February 2026.

In fact, an earlier NRI report states that a single CBG plant can eliminate 11,000-12,000 kilograms of PM emissions annually, which is equivalent to emission savings from 1.5-1.75 lac EVs or that achieved by removing 25000 older vehicles from the roads.

The agricultural lens matters because of the feedstock issue. Punjab and Haryana together produce about 29 million tonnes of paddy straw, which are sometimes burnt because the window for sowing wheat after the paddy harvest is extremely short. While the official picture on emissions from stubble has improved, tens of millions of tonnes of residue need a permanent, paying destination, that fines and machines cannot supply.

A CBG plant offers farmers a price for straw instead of a penalty for burning it, villages get a local employer and soil a nutrient-rich digestate. While policy has helped in building demand—blending obligations is set at 1 per cent in 2025-26, 3  per cent in 2026-27, 4 per cent in 2027-28 and 5  per cent from 2028-29 yet existing plants are reported to run at only 20 to 60  per cent of capacity, The reason: feedstock is seasonal and collection is fragmented and year-round aggregation of biomass, long-term offtake contracts and simpler clearances would change that.

None of this competes with the electric future. Electrons for two- and three-wheelers and urban fleets, increasingly green gas for heavier, high-mileage vehicles, and the farm as supplier of one and beneficiary of the other. The test is not which technology wins but whether every vehicle runs on the cleanest energy available to it.
India’s mobility transition will not only be decided in showrooms and power stations, but in the fields, by what we do with the straw left behind after harvest.

title: EVs, CNG and CBG: Why India’s clean mobility transition also needs an agricultural lens
